connection: Domain repository contracts and in-memory implementations are complete. Infrastructure references Domain but still contains only its template placeholder. Add EF Core persistence to Infrastructure without moving storage concerns into Domain.
objectives: Explain the real gap this session fills: the source app's real ClockEntryRepository has no persistence beyond an in-memory list that is discarded when the process exits.
Read PayrollDbContext : DbContext as this codebase's first genuinely framework-required inheritance, previewed in Session 19.
Map ClockEntryEntity's fields to ClockEntry's real properties, and explain why the entity is a separate type rather than reusing ClockEntry directly.
Explain what 'change tracking' means concretely: db.ClockEntries.Add(entity) marks the entity as Added before SaveChangesAsync ever runs.

visuals.title: The real gap: no persistence beyond one process's lifetime
visuals.explanation: ClockEntryRepository's real _clockEntries list exists only in memory -- restarting the cumulative TimeClock application loses every clocked-in employee. PayrollDbContext fills this real, unaddressed gap.

visuals.title: PayrollDbContext : DbContext -- required inheritance, not chosen
visuals.explanation: EF Core requires your context type to literally be a DbContext; there is no interface-based alternative for this specific framework capability.

visuals.title: ClockEntryEntity mirrors ClockEntry's shape, but is a distinct type
visuals.explanation: EmployeeId, ClockIn, ClockOut are copied field-for-field from the real ClockEntry -- but ClockEntryEntity is EF Core's storage-shaped type, not the domain's behavior-shaped ClockEntry.

visuals.title: Add marks an entity tracked before anything is saved
visuals.explanation: db.ClockEntries.Add(entity) changes the entity's EntityState to Added immediately -- SaveChangesAsync later translates every tracked change into the actual database write.

preQuiz.prompt: What happens to every ClockEntry the real console app has recorded when the process exits?
options: All of it is lost -- ClockEntryRepository's real storage is an in-memory List<ClockEntry> with no persistence to disk or a database
It is automatically saved to a local file
Nothing -- the learner solution already uses EF Core
preQuiz.explanation: This is a real, verified gap in cumulative learner solution -- confirmed by reading Repositories/ClockEntryRepository.cs, which has no persistence mechanism at all.

preQuiz.prompt: Why must PayrollDbContext be declared as a class that inherits from DbContext, rather than just implementing an interface?
options: EF Core's design requires your context type to literally extend DbContext to gain its real infrastructure (DbSet<T> properties, change tracking, SaveChangesAsync) -- there is no interface-only way to opt into that machinery
It is a stylistic preference this course chose
preQuiz.explanation: This is the genuinely framework-required inheritance Session 19 previewed -- the first inheritance relationship in this codebase that isn't a deliberate teaching choice.

preQuiz.prompt: What does db.ClockEntries.Add(entity) do before SaveChangesAsync is ever called?
options: It marks the entity as tracked with EntityState.Added -- SaveChangesAsync later reads every tracked entity's state to decide what SQL to generate
It immediately writes the entity to the database
Nothing -- Add has no effect until SaveChangesAsync runs
preQuiz.explanation: Change tracking is exactly this: EF Core records what changed in memory first, then translates the accumulated changes into database operations only when SaveChangesAsync is explicitly called.

concept.title: A real gap, honestly named
paragraphs: Nothing in cumulative learner solution persists a ClockEntry anywhere beyond process memory. Every employee's clock-in and clock-out history is gone the moment the console app exits.

This session does not claim EF Core already exists in the production code -- it builds PayrollDbContext specifically because that gap is real, and giving IClockEntryRepository a second, database-backed implementation is the natural next step once the gap is visible.

concept.title: PayrollDbContext: the entity, the context, and change tracking
paragraphs: PayrollDbContext(DbContextOptions<PayrollDbContext> options) : DbContext(options) exposes DbSet<ClockEntryEntity> ClockEntries -- EF Core's queryable, trackable representation of a database table.

ClockEntryEntity deliberately mirrors ClockEntry's real fields (EmployeeId, ClockIn, ClockOut) plus an Id primary key EF Core needs -- it is a separate, storage-shaped type, not a reuse of the domain's ClockEntry class.

concept.title: Why a separate entity, not ClockEntry itself
paragraphs: ClockEntry's real constructor takes only employeeId and clockIn, and ClockOut has a private setter -- both deliberate domain invariants (Session 6-7). EF Core needs to construct and populate ClockEntryEntity freely (including an Id it generates), which would conflict with those same invariants if forced onto ClockEntry directly.
Keeping them separate means ClockEntry's domain rules stay exactly as strict as Sessions 5-24 established, while ClockEntryEntity is free to be exactly as permissive as EF Core's mapping needs.

lab.objective: Add EF Core persistence to Infrastructure without moving storage concerns into Domain.
lab.title: Persist Clock Entries through EF Core
lab.task: Create an EF Core-backed repository in Infrastructure and prove with SQLite that a clock-entry row survives beyond one DbContext instance.
lab.startingCondition: Domain repository contracts and in-memory implementations are complete. Infrastructure references Domain but still contains only its template placeholder.
steps: Open src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure and confirm Class1.cs is still only the template placeholder.
Delete src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure/Class1.cs.
Add the Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore package to the Infrastructure project.
Add the Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite package to the Infrastructure project.
Add the SQLite EF Core package required by integration tests to the Domain.Tests project.
Add a ProjectReference from Domain.Tests to PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure.
Create src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure/ClockEntryEntity.cs.
In ClockEntryEntity.cs, declare a public sealed class named ClockEntryEntity.
Add Id, EmployeeId, ClockIn, and nullable ClockOut properties shaped for persistence.
Create src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure/TimeClockDbContext.cs.
In TimeClockDbContext.cs, declare a public sealed TimeClockDbContext class deriving from DbContext.
Add a constructor that accepts DbContextOptions<TimeClockDbContext> and passes options to the base constructor.
Add a DbSet<ClockEntryEntity> property named ClockEntries.
Create src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure/EfClockEntryRepository.cs.
In EfClockEntryRepository.cs, declare a public sealed class named EfClockEntryRepository that implements IClockEntryRepository.
Add a private readonly TimeClockDbContext field and assign it through constructor injection.
In the save method, map the Domain ClockEntry values to a new ClockEntryEntity without adding EF attributes to ClockEntry.
Add the new entity to TimeClockDbContext.ClockEntries.
Call SaveChangesAsync with the supplied CancellationToken.
Implement the required lookup by filtering ClockEntryEntity rows before materialization.
Map each materialized ClockEntryEntity back to the existing Domain ClockEntry contract.
Create tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests/TimeClockDbContextTests.cs.
In the integration test, open one in-memory SQLite connection and keep it open for the test lifetime.
Create DbContextOptions<TimeClockDbContext> that use that open SQLite connection.
Create the database schema with EnsureCreatedAsync.
Add one ClockEntryEntity and assert that its EntityState is Added before SaveChangesAsync.
Call SaveChangesAsync, query the row through a fresh context, and assert its persisted values.
Run the focused TimeClockDbContextTests and then the full solution test suite.
lab.expectedBehavior: Infrastructure persists entries through EF Core while Domain remains storage-agnostic.

commit: session-30: teach ef core context entities and tracking
review: The lab uses production because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: If ClockEntryEntity were removed and ClockEntry were used directly as the EF Core entity, what real conflict would arise?
options: EF Core needs to construct ClockEntry objects and assign an Id/ClockOut freely when materializing query results, which conflicts with ClockEntry's real constructor (no Id parameter) and ClockOut's private setter
There would be no conflict -- EF Core can use any class as an entity
ClockEntry would need to become an interface
postQuiz.explanation: This is the concrete, specific reason for the separate entity type -- not a generic 'always separate your layers' rule, but a real conflict between EF Core's needs and ClockEntry's real domain invariants.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does db.Entry(entity).State change from Added to Unchanged only after SaveChangesAsync, not immediately after Add?
options: Add only registers the entity with the context's in-memory change tracker; SaveChangesAsync is the operation that actually executes the database write and then updates tracking to reflect the now-persisted, unchanged state
State never changes -- this is a bug in EF Core
Add and SaveChangesAsync do the same thing
postQuiz.explanation: This two-step behavior -- track first, persist on demand -- is exactly what allows EntryCompletion's validation (Session 24) to run before anything reaches the database (Session 35's workflow).

postQuiz.prompt: Does adding PayrollDbContext change anything about the real, in-memory ClockEntryRepository or its consumers (ClockEntryService, PayrollService)?
options: No -- PayrollDbContext is a new, separate, alternative implementation of persistence; the real ClockEntryRepository and every class depending on IClockEntryRepository continue to work exactly as before
Yes -- ClockEntryRepository is deleted and replaced
postQuiz.explanation: This session adds a new capability alongside the real, unmodified source code -- exactly the 'clearly-labeled extension' framing the task's own instructions call for.

reflections: Why does this session build a new entity type instead of trying to make ClockEntry itself EF Core-compatible?
What would you need to change about PayrollDbContext to make it usable as a real, additional implementation of IClockEntryRepository, alongside the existing in-memory one?
Where else in this codebase might a domain type's strict invariants make it a poor fit for direct use as a persistence entity?
whatBreaks: Constructing ClockEntryEntity with EF Core's usual pattern (a parameterless constructor plus property setters) would fail if attempted against ClockEntry directly, since ClockEntry's real constructor requires employeeId and clockIn and ClockOut cannot be set from outside ClockOutEmployee. Skipping SaveChangesAsync after Add leaves the entity tracked as Added but never actually written to the database -- a common source of 'why didn't my data save' bugs when the two steps are conflated.
summary: The real cumulative learner solution has no persistence beyond an in-memory List<ClockEntry> -- a genuine, verified gap. PayrollDbContext : DbContext is this codebase's first framework-required inheritance (previewed in Session 19), and ClockEntryEntity is a deliberately separate, storage-shaped type -- not a reuse of ClockEntry -- because ClockEntry's real domain invariants (constructor shape, private ClockOut setter) would conflict with how EF Core needs to construct and populate entities.
